lines.text: A narrow strip of West Africa, ruled by Germany and then France, and by one family for more than half a century. This is the story of Togo.
In 1884 Germany claimed the coast and the land behind it as a colony, Togoland.
Sylvanus Olympio would grow up to lead the fight for freedom and become the country's first president.
In the First World War, Britain and France seized the colony and split it. France ruled the eastern part for over forty years.
Gnassingbe Eyadema, a soldier, would seize power in 1967 and rule for nearly four decades.
In 1960 Togo became independent. Three years later Olympio was killed in a coup.
When Eyadema died in 2005, his son Faure took his place, and in 2025 became president of the council.
On the football pitch, the striker Emmanuel Adebayor took Togo to its only World Cup, in 2006.
In the north, the Batammariba people's land of earthen tower houses, Koutammakou, became a World Heritage Site in 2004.
From German colony to independent state, Togo's story is still unfolding.
